paras: The threatened lynching of Andrew Gilford took place in Mendota, Illinois, in early July 1903, when crowds talked of lynching Gilford, a Black man from Princeton jailed for stabbing a white man, Albert Kane. Mayor Brown swore in special police, who dispersed a mob at the jail and kept it under heavy guard. A wire dispatch carried the story under the headline "Another Outbreak of the Mob Spirit."

Kane, described as white and from Meriden, five miles east of Mendota, was "seriously stabbed" by Gilford, described as "colored" and from Princeton. According to the dispatch, the stabbing came out of a quarrel with "another colored man named Bennett." Gilford and Bennett were both placed in jail.

Because Kane was popular, the dispatch said, "crowds of men congregated and marched around the town talking of lynching." A mob then gathered around the jail. Mayor Brown swore in a number of special police, the mob was dispersed, and the jail was heavily guarded. The report describes no attempt to break into the jail and no injury to either prisoner.
The coverage does not report Kane's condition after the stabbing, nor any hearing, indictment or trial for Gilford or Bennett.

The story reached print as a single wire dispatch dated Mendota, July 7. The Rock Island Argus ran it on its front page that day under "Another Outbreak of the Mob Spirit," in a roundup headed "Another Mob on Hand" with mob stories from Sioux City, Iowa, and Vincennes, Indiana. The Grant County Herald of Lancaster, Wisconsin, printed the same text word for word on its front page the next day.

Both papers identified Kane as "white" and Gilford and Bennett as "colored," stated the stabbing as fact, and called the crowd at the jail a "mob." Neither added comment of its own, and no Black-press report of the episode was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Andrew Gilford
bases: Crowds marched through Mendota 'talking of lynching' a Black man jailed for stabbing a white man, and a mob gathered at the jail before special police dispersed it; no one was taken or harmed (A1).

A crowd talked of lynching Andrew Gilford and gathered at the jail, which meets the group and pretext elements, but the mob was dispersed and no one was killed (A1); this was a threatened lynching only.
The only coverage is one wire dispatch from Mendota printed verbatim in two papers (A1, A2), so there is no independent second report.
